PART 2 — SETS
Weeks 11–12
The uploaded Week 11–12 material is specifically the SETS topic.
2.1 What is a Set?
Both logic and sets are the foundation on which the rest of discrete mathematics is built.
“A sets are collections of distinct objects.”
The set of natural numbers are the “whole numbers”:
0,1,2,3,…

Example
A={1ⓜ,2ⓜ,3}

Elements of a Set
The objects inside a set are called Elements.
Symbol:
∈

Example:
2∈A

2.2 Set Construction
Constructing is the process of describing a set by specifying its elements that determine which elements belong to the set.
There are three ways to construct a set:
	Roster method
	Set-builder notation
	Interval notation
Roster Method
The roster method defines a set by listing all of its elements, separated by commas and enclosed in braces {┤}.
Example:
A={1ⓜ,2ⓜ,3ⓜ,4ⓜ,5}

Set-Builder Notation
The set-builder notation defines a set by describing a property or rule that its elements must satisfy.
Format:
{x∣"condition on " x}

Example:
B={x∣x" is an even integer and " x<10}

Interval Notation
Interval notation is used to represent sets of real number that lie between two endpoints.
Symbols:

(┤)— endpoint not included
	[┤]— endpoint included
Examples:
(1ⓜ,5)

All real numbers between 1 and 5, excluding 1 and 5.
[2ⓜ,6]

All real numbers from 2 to 6, including both.
(-ⓜ,∞3]

All real numbers less than or equal to 3.

2.3 Set Operations
Set operations are actions used to combine, compare, or separate elements of two or more sets.
Three most common set operations:
	Union (∪)
	Intersection (∩)
	Difference (-)
1. Union (∪)
The union of two sets contains all elements that are in either set or in both set.
A∪B

= elements in A or B.
Example:
A={1ⓜ,3ⓜ,5}
B={1ⓜ,2ⓜ,6}

Therefore:
A∪B={1ⓜ,2ⓜ,3ⓜ,5ⓜ,6}

2. Intersection (∩)
The intersection of two sets contains only the elements that are common to both sets.
A∩B

= common elements.

2.4 Types of Sets
There are four types presented:
	Empty Set (Null Set)
	Finite Set
	Infinite Set
	Universal Set
1. Empty Set (Null Set)
An empty set is a set that contains no elements.
Symbols:
∅

or
{┤}

Example:
A={┤}

or
A=∅

2. Finite Set
A finite set is a set that contains a limited or countable number of elements.
Example:
B={1ⓜ,2ⓜ,3ⓜ,4ⓜ,5}

3. Infinite Set
An infinite set is a set that contains an unlimited number of elements and cannot be completely listed.
Example:
C={1ⓜ,2ⓜ,3ⓜ,4ⓜ,5ⓜ,…}

The set of natural numbers.
4. Universal Set
A universal set is the set that contains all elements under discussion for a particular problem.
Symbol:
U

Example:
U={1ⓜ,2ⓜ,3ⓜ,4ⓜ,5ⓜ,6ⓜ,7ⓜ,8}
A={4ⓜ,6ⓜ,7ⓜ,8}
B={1ⓜ,2ⓜ,3ⓜ,7ⓜ,8}

Then, Ucontains all possible elements in that context.

2.5 Subsets
A subset is a set whose all elements are contained in another set.
Symbols:
⊆

means subset of or equal to.
⊂

means proper subset (subset but not equal).
Example
Let:
X={10ⓜ,20ⓜ,30}
Y={10ⓜ,20ⓜ,30ⓜ,40}

All elements of X are in Y.
X≠Y

Therefore:
X⊂Y
